title: Fidelity signal map: int6 probe (working notes)
content:
Goal:
- Get an empirical 'signal map' that shows which prompt-slices and quality signals are most sensitive across a continuum of precision (int8 -> int6 -> int4) and algorithm (per-channel AWQ vs layerwise GPTQ).
- Provide a lightweight rubric for whether int6 is a cost/quality sweet spot for onboarding certain customer workloads.

Background / motivation:
- Most onboarding notes focus on int8 vs int4 and AWQ/GPTQ comparisons. We suspect there's a useful operating point between int8 and int4 (roughly int6) for many families that reduces cost but avoids the major tail-case fidelity drops. This doc is a quick, informal probe to map where signal degradation appears as precision is reduced.

Quick experiment summary (setup):
- Models: open-model-arch-v2 (base), open-model-arch-v2-chat (chat variant) — same weights, different tokenizers/EOStok.
- Quant paths: baseline FP16, int8 (per-channel), int6 (experimental per-channel via AWQ-like calibration with 6-bit mantissa emulation), int4 (AWQ and GPTQ separately).
- Calibration: 2k random in-domain prompts for activation calibration; also per-slice calibration variants (see notes).
- Prompt sets: 7 slices curated from onboarding prompt bank: short-instruction, multi-step-reasoning, code-gen-small, code-gen-long, domain-knowledge-fact, conversational-followup, multilingual-EN-ES. Each slice = 200 prompts (mix of seed+perturbations).
- Evaluation signals: exact-match-esque (where relevant), n-gram BLEU for code/comments, embedding-similarity (cosine) to FP16 responses, reported hallucination rate (human-annotated subset), runtime latency and peak memory, top-k token KL to FP16, and a scalar "acceptability" from crowd labels (0/1).
- Runs: deterministic decoding (top-p 0.95, temp 0.0 for factual; temp 0.7 for chat where applicable).

Preliminary numbers (high-level deltas vs FP16) — NOTE: these are initial probe values, small N; please don't treat as final:
- int8 (per-channel): avg embedding cosine drop ≈ -0.9% overall; hallucination +0.8pp; latency -9% token throughput gain.
- int6 (experimental): avg embedding cosine drop ≈ -2.4%; hallucination +2.5pp concentrated in multi-step-reasoning and code-gen-long; latency -18% token throughput gain (roughly linear between int8 and int4).
- int4 (AWQ/GPTQ mixed): avg embedding cosine drop ≈ -6.8%; hallucination +8.2pp; severe deltas on multi-step reasoning and some domain-knowledge prompts.

Slice-level observations (qualitative):
- short-instruction: robust down to int6; user-acceptable in most cases. Small tone/style changes; few hallucinations.
- multi-step-reasoning: sensitive — int6 introduces coherence breaks about 10–12% of the time in our sample (compared to ~3% at int8). Int4 catastrophic for longer chains.
- code-gen-small: okay at int6 for short functions; formatting and minor off-by-one errors increase.
- code-gen-long: int6 shows increased truncation/incorrect state handling (larger KL on token tails). GPTQ performed worse than AWQ here, possibly due to layerwise rounding artifacts.
- domain-knowledge-fact: factual retrieval mostly stable at int6 except for low-frequency facts; int4 shows spikes of hallucination.
- conversational-followup: degredation subtle; more repetition and token-level collapse occasionally at int4.
- multilingual-EN-ES: int6 keeps basic fluency but morphological errors increase; int4 produces more literal translations and occasionally dropped accents.

Signal mapping idea (how we visualize):
- For each slice, compute a small vector of deltas: [embedding-cosine-diff, hallucination-pp, acceptability-diff, KL-div, latency%].
- Normalize per-signal to z-scores across slices.
- Plot slices on a 2D map using PCA on those z-vectors; overlay arrow fields showing direction from int8->int6->int4.
- Clinically inspect which signals dominate each axis (makes map interpretable).

Early interpretations / heuristics: 
- Int6 seems to preserve a majority of short-form and retrieval-style capabilities while offering 10–20% cost reduction vs int8 in our runtime. It's not a universal win; failure modes concentrate on long-context reasoning and some long-code generation.
- AWQ-style per-channel quantization with enhanced calibration (slice-aware) reduced frequency of hallucination spikes vs naive per-tensor schemes.
- GPTQ still beats AWQ in some reproducible microbenchmarks (e.g., specific transformer block sensitivity in token-prediction heads) but is more brittle when sequence length rises — probably due to per-layer quant noise accumulation.

Notable failure cases (examples):
- Prompt (multi-step): "Plan a 6-step troubleshooting checklist for a flaky network adapter that disconnects intermittently when idle."
  - FP16: coherent 6-step checklist with conditional checks.
  - int6: step 4 conflates device and driver steps, suggests re-installing wrong package — subtle but failure for automation.
  - int4: invents a nonexistent CLI tool name (hallucination).

- Prompt (code-gen-long): large sorting-with-state function.
  - FP16: correct loop + state handling.
  - int6: off-by-one index in inner loop.
  - int4: returns incomplete function.

Operational notes (practical onboarding implications):
- Customer tiering: for customers using short instruction / retrieval tasks, int6 could be offered as a "balanced" serving profile (lower cost) with an explicit note about multi-step/code caveats.
- Canary design: include slice-targeted canaries (a small set of high-value prompts from each customer) and monitor embedding-cosine + acceptability. If either drops beyond threshold (e.g., cosine -3% and acceptability -6pp), auto-roll back to int8.
- Calibration: run calibration on a mix of generic + per-customer small calibration sets. Slice-aware calibration reduced problem prompts by ~30% in our probe.

Open questions / next experiments:
1) Bigger N: scale each slice from 200->2k prompts and re-evaluate. Some int6 failure modes are low-frequency and need larger samples.
2) Calibration ablations: test calibration sizes (1k, 2k, 5k), and test per-layer vs global bias correction.
3) Tokenization sensitivity: does tokenizer normalization (esp. languages with diacritics) amplify int6 errors? Run separate tokenizer ablation.
4) AWQ hyperparams: explore clipping thresholds and per-channel zero-point optimizations for int6.
5) GPTQ variants: try hybrid pipeline (GPTQ for first N layers, AWQ for last M) to see whether accumulation can be reduced.
6) Human-level acceptance: run larger human eval (>1k annot) on high-risk slices to get tighter error bars for business decisions.

Actionable next steps (short term):
- T1: Expand probe to 2k prompts per slice (owner: Ben Liu) — target ~2 weeks.
- T2: Build the signal-map visualization notebook and add arrow animation for int8->int6->int4 transitions (owner: Maya) — 1 week prototype.
- T3: Wire simple canary policy prototype in serving console: per-deployment profile option to enable "int6-balanced" with auto-fallback (owner: Jordan) — prototype 2 weeks.

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- Keep naming distinct from our int4/int8 reports (this doc intentionally focuses on the continuous trajectory and mapping).
- Consider adding a small section of cost-per-token estimates with throughput-normalized economics (to present to PMs).
- This doc is intentionally informal: will convert into a polished onboarding checklist if results hold.
